key_terms.term: First law for a closed system (process form)
key_terms.meaning: Q − W = ΔU = U₂ − U₁, where Q is heat added to the system, W is work done by the system, and U is internal energy; all in joules or kJ
∮Q = ∮W, that is, net heat supplied equals net work delivered when the system returns to its starting state
Heat added to the system and work done by the system are positive; heat rejected and work done on the system are negative
The sum of all microscopic kinetic and potential energies of the molecules of a fixed mass; a state property measured in kJ
H = U + pV, where p is pressure and V is volume; the energy that includes flow work, measured in kJ
cv is heat per kg per K at constant volume (raises U); cp is heat per kg per K at constant pressure (raises H); units kJ/(kg·K)
cp − cv = R for an ideal gas, where R is the gas constant in kJ/(kg·K)
γ = cp/cv, also called the adiabatic index; about 1.4 for air
A process obeying pVⁿ = C, where n is the polytropic index and C is a constant
A process at constant temperature, given by pV = C, that is, polytropic with n = 1
A process with no heat transfer (Q = 0), given by pV^γ = C for an ideal gas
A constant-volume process (n = ∞) in which work done is zero and Q = ΔU
A constant-pressure process (n = 0) in which work done is p(V₂ − V₁) and Q = ΔH
Perpetual motion machine of the first kind: a device that would deliver work with no energy input, or more work than the heat supplied
h₁ + V₁²/2 + gz₁ + q = h₂ + V₂²/2 + gz₂ + w, where h is specific enthalpy, V velocity, z elevation, q and w heat and work per kg
A fixed region in space through which mass may flow; the open system used for turbines, pumps and nozzles
A duct of decreasing area in which fluid speeds up; q ≈ 0 and w = 0, so enthalpy drop becomes kinetic energy
A duct of increasing area that slows fluid down and raises its pressure, a nozzle running in reverse
A restriction with q = 0 and w = 0; enthalpy stays constant across it (h₁ = h₂) while pressure falls
The first law only counts energy; it gives no direction of flow and cannot rule out a PMM-2 or explain why heat flows hot to cold

takeaways: For a closed system Q − W = ΔU, and over a full cycle the net heat equals the net work, because the system comes back to the same U.
Internal energy is stored inside the matter and is fixed by the state; enthalpy H = U + pV adds the flow work and is the natural property for open systems.
For an ideal gas cp − cv = R and γ = cp/cv, so measuring γ and R gives both specific heats without any table.
Any closed process that follows pVⁿ = C can be handled with one work formula, W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1), and n = 0, 1, γ, ∞ reproduce isobaric, isothermal, adiabatic and isochoric processes.
A PMM-1 would create energy from nothing; the first law forbids it, which is the practical use of the law as a check on any proposed device.
The steady flow energy equation balances enthalpy, kinetic energy, potential energy, heat and work per kilogram of flowing fluid.
In a nozzle, diffuser or throttle the work term vanishes, so the equation collapses into a simple exchange between enthalpy and velocity, or into h₁ = h₂.
The first law is a book-keeping rule, not a direction-finder; the second law is needed to say which energy-conserving processes can actually happen.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually ask for a full statement of the first law with sign convention, a first-law analysis of a named device (turbine, nozzle, boiler, throttle) using the steady flow energy equation, and a short discussion of PMM-1 and the limits of the first law.

bank.q: State the first law of thermodynamics for a closed system undergoing (a) a process and (b) a complete cycle. Explain the sign convention you use, and show that the two statements are consistent.
outline: Write Q − W = U₂ − U₁ with every symbol and unit defined.
Write the cycle form ∮Q = ∮W and explain that U returns to its initial value so ΔU = 0.
State the sign convention: heat in and work out positive.
Show that summing the process form over the steps of a cycle gives the cycle form.

bank.q: Define internal energy and enthalpy. Derive H = U + pV and explain why enthalpy, and not internal energy, appears in flow devices such as boilers and turbines.
outline: Internal energy as the microscopic energy stored in a fixed mass; a state property.
Definition H = U + pV with units kJ and specific enthalpy h in kJ/kg.
Flow work pV as the work a fluid does pushing its way into and out of a control volume.
Hence the energy carried by a flowing stream per kg is h + V²/2 + gz.

bank.q: Explain why cp is always greater than cv for a gas, and derive cp − cv = R for an ideal gas.
outline: At constant volume no expansion work is done, so all heat raises U.
At constant pressure the gas expands and also does pΔV work, so more heat is needed.
First law at constant pressure: qp = ΔU + pΔV = ΔH.
Use pV = RT for 1 kg and ΔU = cvΔT to get cp − cv = R.
Mention that for solids and liquids cp ≈ cv because expansion is tiny.

bank.q: Define a perpetual motion machine of the first kind and state why the first law forbids it. Give two devices that people have claimed to be PMM-1 and explain the flaw.
outline: Definition: delivers work with no energy input, or more work than heat supplied.
First law for a cycle: W_net cannot exceed Q_net.
Efficiency greater than 100 percent means W > Q, which would need ΔU to keep falling forever.
Take any claimed machine and show its energy balance fails; note friction and losses make real efficiency lower still.

bank.q: One kilogram of air at 500 kPa and 0.2 m³ expands to 100 kPa along pV^1.3 = C. Take R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K) and γ = 1.4. Find the final volume, the work done, the heat transferred, and the change in internal energy.
outline: Use p₁V₁ⁿ = p₂V₂ⁿ to get V₂ = V₁(p₁/p₂)^(1/n).
Work W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1), with pressures in kPa and volumes in m³ to get kJ.
Temperatures from pV = mRT, then ΔU = m cv (T₂ − T₁) with cv = R/(γ − 1).
First law: Q = ΔU + W, and state whether heat is added or rejected.

bank.q: A gas is compressed isothermally from 100 kPa, 0.5 m³ to 500 kPa. Find the work and heat transfer, and compare with the work needed if the same compression were adiabatic between the same two pressures.
outline: Isothermal: W = p₁V₁ ln(p₁/p₂), negative for compression.
ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas at constant T, so Q = W.
Adiabatic work from (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(γ − 1) with V₂ = V₁(p₁/p₂)^(1/γ).
Compare magnitudes and explain that the adiabatic path ends hotter, so more work is spent.

bank.q: Steam enters a turbine at 3 MPa and 350 °C with a velocity of 60 m/s and leaves at 20 kPa with a velocity of 150 m/s and a dryness fraction of 0.92. The heat loss from the casing is 12 kJ per kg of steam. Find the work output per kg.
outline: Choose the turbine as a control volume with steady flow.
Write the SFEE with q = −12 kJ/kg and no elevation change.
Look up h₁ from superheated steam tables at 3 MPa, 350 °C; h₂ from hf + x·hfg at 20 kPa.
Solve w = (h₁ − h₂) + (V₁² − V₂²)/2000 + q, taking care with the 1000 in the kinetic term to get kJ/kg.

bank.q: Air enters a nozzle at 400 K and 30 m/s and leaves at 300 K. Treat air as an ideal gas with cp = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K) and assume the nozzle is adiabatic with no work transfer. Find the exit velocity.
outline: SFEE with q = 0, w = 0 and negligible height change.
h₁ + V₁²/2 = h₂ + V₂²/2.
Replace h₁ − h₂ by cp(T₁ − T₂); watch units: divide V² by 2000 to convert to kJ/kg.
Solve V₂ = √(V₁² + 2cp(T₁ − T₂)·1000).

bank.q: A refrigerant passes through an expansion valve from saturated liquid at 800 kPa to 200 kPa. Show that the process is isenthalpic and find the exit quality. State every assumption.
outline: Control volume around the valve: q = 0, w = 0, and changes in kinetic and potential energy are neglected.
SFEE then gives h₁ = h₂.
h₁ = hf at 800 kPa; h₂ = hf + x·hfg at 200 kPa.
Solve for x and comment that throttling is irreversible even though enthalpy is constant.

bank.q: A closed system is proposed to follow a cycle in which the net work output is 200 kJ while the net heat supplied is 150 kJ. Using the first law, examine the claim and state what you must check before rejecting it.
outline: For a cycle ΔU = 0, hence ∮Q = ∮W.
The proposal has ∮W > ∮Q, so it violates the first law.
Check whether the system returns exactly to its initial state and whether all heat and work terms were counted, including surroundings.
Conclude that the device is a PMM-1 and no design of bearings or materials can make it work.

bank.q: Compare the work produced by isothermal and adiabatic expansion of the same ideal gas from the same initial state to the same final pressure. Explain which path gives more work and where the missing energy goes.
outline: Both arrive at the same pressure; plot both on a p–V diagram and compare areas.
Isothermal expansion at constant T gives W = p₁V₁ ln(p₁/p₂).
Adiabatic expansion ends at a lower temperature, ΔU is negative, so part of the work comes from internal energy and the area is smaller.
State that the isothermal path requires heat input from a reservoir, which is why it delivers more work.

bank.q: A rigid insulated tank is divided into two parts by a thin membrane, one side holding high-pressure air and the other a vacuum. The membrane bursts. Using the first law, determine the final temperature, and explain why this result is the same whatever the gas.
outline: Control volume is the whole tank: q = 0, w = 0 (rigid, insulated), no mass crosses.
First law gives ΔU = 0, so U₂ = U₁.
For an ideal gas U depends on T only, so T₂ = T₁.
Note that pressure and volume change, entropy rises, and the process is irreversible, but the first law alone tells us nothing about that.

bank.q: State the limitations of the first law of thermodynamics. Use a paddle-wheel experiment and a hot cup of tea on a table to show what the first law does not tell us.
outline: List: no direction of process, no quality of energy, no test for feasibility other than energy balance, cannot rule out PMM-2.
Work turning fully into heat (paddle wheel) and heat never turning fully into work in a cycle, though both conserve energy.
Heat flows from hot tea to the room and never the reverse, with no energy balance violation either way.
Conclude that a second law is required, and mention that entropy and the Kelvin-Planck statement supply it.

bank.q: Air flows steadily through a compressor, is cooled in a heat exchanger, then passes through a throttle. Write the SFEE for each device, state which terms drop out and why, and combine the three into one statement about the whole flow path.
outline: Compressor: q small or given, w negative (work input), velocity and height neglected, so w = h₂ − h₁ + q.
Heat exchanger: w = 0, no work, no change in kinetic or potential energy, so q = h₃ − h₂.
Throttle: q = 0, w = 0, so h₄ = h₃.
Combine to relate shaft work input to the change in enthalpy of the stream and the heat removed.
Note each device is steady flow with uniform properties at inlet and outlet.

glossary.def: The fixed quantity of matter or the region in space chosen for study.
Everything outside the system boundary that can interact with the system.
A system with a fixed mass across whose boundary only heat and work can pass, not matter.
A region fixed in space, with mass allowed to cross its boundary, used for open systems.
The complete set of properties of a system at one instant.
A measurable quantity that depends only on the state, such as pressure, temperature or volume.
A change of state from one equilibrium state to another.
A sequence of processes that returns the system to its initial state.
Energy transferred across a boundary because of a temperature difference.
Energy transferred across a boundary as a force acting through a displacement, or by any non-heat means.
A quantity whose value depends on how a process is carried out; heat and work are path functions.
A quantity fixed by the state alone, independent of history; internal energy and enthalpy are state functions.
The microscopic energy stored within the matter of a system, denoted U.
The combination H = U + pV, useful whenever mass flows across a boundary.
The heat required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one kelvin.
The constant in pV = mRT, equal to the universal gas constant divided by the molar mass.
The exponent n in pVⁿ = C, which fixes the shape of the process path.
A process or boundary with zero heat transfer.
A process carried out at constant temperature.
A process carried out at constant pressure.
A process carried out at constant volume.
A passage of reducing area that increases fluid velocity at the expense of enthalpy.
A passage of increasing area that converts kinetic energy into pressure.
Flow through a restriction with no heat or work transfer, so enthalpy is constant.
Flow in which mass and energy within the control volume do not change with time.
A hypothetical device that produces work with no energy input, forbidden by the first law.
